stories.headline: Update: Justice Department Sues California to Block Counting of About 20,000 Ballots
stories.summary:
The Justice Department sued California and two election officials on Thursday. It asked a federal court to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots cast by about 20,000 voters it suspects are not U.S. citizens, at least until their citizenship status is confirmed. The suit follows a demand sent Tuesday giving the state 48 hours to act.

According to coverage of the filing, the department gave California and local officials a USB drive containing names it said were drawn from Department of Homeland Security information. It demanded that they compare those names against state voter rolls and segregate any ballots from noncitizens. The Los Angeles County clerk said the county would not access the drive, and the deadline passed before the department filed suit. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release, "State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America."

California officials blasted the lawsuit. The Guardian described the underlying demand as specious and noted that it follows earlier claims of noncitizen voting that have been debunked. State and local officials have not accepted the department's list as proof that noncitizens were improperly registered or sent ballots. Supporters of the administration's approach argue that federal data should be checked against voter rolls before ballots are tabulated. Critics say the move threatens eligible voters' ballots and is a pressure tactic weeks before the midterms.

The case now goes to a federal judge, who must decide quickly given the approaching election. Early voting begins soon in many states, and election officials say they worry that unsubstantiated claims could be used to contest results in November.

stories.headline: North Korea and China Open New Yalu River Bridge After 12-Year Delay
stories.summary:
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media reported. The New Yalu River Bridge spans about 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea. It is expected to become the main land route for trade between the two countries.

The bridge was initially slated to open in 2014, but the launch was postponed indefinitely after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities as relations with Beijing cooled. In a video address on Thursday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang called it a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea" and said the countries were "opening a new chapter" in ties. A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson called it an important facility for connectivity.

China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons program. Bilateral trade reached $2.7 billion last year, recovering to pre-pandemic levels and driven mostly by Chinese exports. Analysts told the BBC that UN sanctions remain in force, so a sudden jump in trade is unlikely. One also said Pyongyang is wary of a flood of Chinese imports that would expand Beijing's influence over its domestic market.

The opening reflects a shift in the relationship. Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing grew impatient with the nuclear program, but China now says little about denuclearization. Observers link this in part to North Korea's closer ties with Russia during the war in Ukraine.

stories.headline: Bus Hits Train at Channel Tunnel Terminal in France, Injuring 19
stories.summary:
A minibus struck a departing freight train on a loading platform at the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel in Coquelles, near Calais, injuring the driver and 18 passengers. French authorities said the collision happened at 19:27 local time on Thursday. The driver and one passenger were severely injured and evacuated by helicopter, though a local official said none of the injuries were life threatening.

The minibus was carrying lorry drivers who were about to board the Le Shuttle vehicle service. Local sub-prefect Agathe Cury said two trains were on either side of the platform, one being loaded by heavy goods vehicles and another, already loaded, that was departing. "For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train," she said. The bus stayed upright, and all of those aboard were men of various nationalities. It is not yet clear whether any were British.

Cury said it was the first time an incident of this type had occurred on an Eurotunnel loading platform. An investigation has begun. After a brief stoppage to evacuate the injured, freight and Eurostar passenger traffic through the tunnel was not disrupted, and Eurostar said its London services were unaffected and would run as scheduled.

stories.headline: Actor Imran Khan Ordered to Leave India After Joining Electoral Reform Protest
stories.summary:
Indian authorities have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by October 28 after he took part in a protest seeking electoral reforms. Khan is an American citizen who holds an Overseas Citizen of India card, which allows people of Indian origin to live in and visit the country but does not confer voting rights. Mumbai police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office served him a notice for violating the law by protesting.

Police said Khan joined a demonstration at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan on October 10, which demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The protest was called by the Cockroach Janta Party, part of a Gen Z-led movement that has held demonstrations for days over allegations of vote fraud, which the election commission denies. Khan was briefly detained along with other protesters. The complaint was filed by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of the governing Bharatiya Janata Party, who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India."

Khan's lawyer says no provision of the law or any rule for card holders prohibits protesting, and the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court. Khan told reporters at the protest: "I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen... to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed." The order comes as he returns to acting this year with a Netflix film after a hiatus of more than a decade.

stories.headline: Update: France Begins Deploying Forces to Help Defend Saudi Oil Facilities as Trump Says Killing Iranian Leaders Complicates Peace
stories.summary:
France is putting into action operational elements of an agreement to help protect Saudi Arabia's oil facilities from attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces, the French Foreign Ministry said Thursday. Spokesperson Pascal Confavreux declined to specify what means had been sent to Saudi Arabia. French President Emmanuel Macron said last month that France would send troops and defense systems to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, a key hub for energy transport.

The announcement signals deeper French involvement in defending Saudi energy infrastructure as Houthi attacks escalate amid the broader Iran war. Saudi Arabia has faced repeated threats to its oil sites and shipping routes from the Yemen-based group. Reuters contributed to the report.

Fox News live coverage also carried remarks from President Trump, who lamented that peace with Iran has become more difficult because Iranian leaders were taken out during the conflict. The story is being covered by 21 outlets across the political spectrum, reflecting the weight of the war on oil prices, the Strait of Hormuz and the approaching midterm elections.

What happens next depends on whether the French deployment deters further Houthi strikes on Saudi energy sites and whether diplomatic channels with Tehran can be reopened.

stories.headline: Federal Lawsuit Accuses Matt Gaetz, Two Others of Sex Trafficking
stories.summary:
Two anonymous women filed a federal civil lawsuit Thursday in the Middle District of Florida accusing former Rep. Matt Gaetz, a Florida Republican, of participating in the sexual exploitation and trafficking of them when they were in their early 20s. The suit also names former Seminole County tax collector Joel Greenberg and former Florida state Rep. Chris Dorworth.

The plaintiffs, identified as Jane Does, allege that the three men coordinated payments, drugs and travel in exchange for sexual acts. Gaetz, who resigned from Congress in November 2024, denied the allegations in a statement to the Guardian and said he would vigorously contest the suit.

The filing is the latest development in a long-running scandal around Gaetz, who has previously denied wrongdoing. Greenberg was earlier convicted in a related federal case. As a civil action, the lawsuit seeks damages rather than criminal penalties, and the allegations have not been tested in court. The case is expected to proceed with responses from the defendants in the coming weeks.

stories.headline: Musk Poured $158 Million Into Texas Senate Race to Rescue Paxton Campaign
stories.summary:
Elon Musk's team contacted Republicans in late August to warn that, without a rapid infusion of money, the party could lose the Texas Senate race within weeks, Axios reported. The discussion set in motion a large rescue effort for Republican Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general, funded substantially by Musk, the party's largest donor.

New federal filings show Musk gave $158 million in September alone to a super PAC backing Paxton, and he was the single donor to the group in the third quarter. The spending revived what had been a sluggish campaign as Musk pushes to preserve Republican majorities in Congress.

The race has tightened in recent weeks, with Democrat James Talarico drawing attention, and midterm ad spending nationwide has passed $10 billion. Republicans view the money as essential to holding a seat once considered safe, while Democrats have pointed to the scale of the donation as evidence of the outsized influence of billionaires in elections. The outcome in Texas could help determine control of the Senate.

stories.headline: Trump Rallies in Montana and Arizona, Renews $5,000 Payment Pledge and Announces Defense Test Range
stories.summary:
President Trump held rallies in Arizona and Kalispell, Montana, as part of a Western midterm campaign blitz that also included stops in Alaska and Ohio this week. He spoke for about an hour and 15 minutes in Montana, where he announced the state would receive a new Defense Department range for testing advanced weapons, including potential autonomous weapons, space and electronic warfare technology, supersonics and hypersonics.

Trump again pledged to send $5,000 to voters if Republicans win Congress in November, adding that recipients would have to spend the money in the United States. Neither he nor the White House has explained how that would be enforced or how the payments would be made. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, plans to introduce legislation to make it happen. Trump warned that a Democratic victory would bring a 1929-style economic depression and promoted the estate tax elimination in the One Big Beautiful Bill, which protects inheritances up to $15 million for individuals.

Critics note Americans rate Trump poorly on the economy amid affordability concerns, and Democrats have questioned the cost and feasibility of the payments. NBC also reported that federal agents seized Rep. Ilhan Omar's phone during a search of her Washington home this week, citing two sources.

stories.headline: Maduro and Wife Plead Not Guilty to New Torture Conspiracy Charges in New York
stories.summary:
Former Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, pleaded not guilty on Thursday to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture. They appeared before Judge Alvin Hellerstein in New York, wearing beige jail uniforms and appearing to have lost weight during detention in Brooklyn. Maduro told the court through a translator that he rejected the indictment entirely and denied the "false accusations and false testimony against me." Hellerstein interrupted and entered a not-guilty plea on his behalf, while Flores said, "I am completely innocent."

Prosecutors added the charges last week, alleging the couple "created and maintained a violent system of repression" in which thousands of Venezuelans were killed, harassed and tortured. The indictment lists methods including electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells and psychological torture. It also alleges that U.S. citizens were among those tortured and that Maduro authorized torture against specific individuals.

The new counts join earlier charges of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons offenses, which also named their son and accomplices and alleged partnerships with cartels designated as terrorist groups. Maduro and Flores were captured in a U.S. military raid in January and taken to New York. Their lawyers argue Maduro, as leader of a sovereign country, has immunity and that seizing him by force was illegal; Maduro has called the charges a pretext for U.S. access to Venezuela's oil reserves.

A judge previously denied Flores's request for release on bond, in which she cited heart problems and other health issues. Trial is scheduled for June 2027, and the sovereign immunity challenges remain pending.

stories.headline: Fired FBI Employees Who Worked on Trump Documents Probe Sue to Regain Jobs
stories.summary:
Nine FBI agents, intelligence analysts and staff operations specialists fired for their roles in the investigation of President Donald Trump's retention of classified documents filed suit Thursday in federal court in Washington seeking reinstatement. The complaint calls their terminations unlawful acts of "political retribution." They were dismissed in February, after earlier firings of agents who worked on the investigation into Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election.

The suit adds to a growing list of legal challenges to mass terminations under FBI Director Kash Patel of agents who took part in investigations of the president or are seen as opposed to administration interests. Patel has said in congressional testimony that those he dismissed had "weaponized" the FBI. The plaintiffs deny that, noting they have more than a century of combined service, including work on the Boston Marathon bombing, hostage recoveries and the investigation of the 2024 assassination attempt on Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania.

Their attorneys, Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio, said the employees "were fired because they did their jobs" and that the suit will "hold the administration accountable for this blatant attack on the rule of law." The complaint also details allegations that Trump stored dozens of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, showed them to unauthorized people and obstructed efforts to retrieve them.

Trump has denied wrongdoing, and the federal case against him was dismissed in 2024 by Judge Aileen Cannon. Administration supporters have defended the firings as a necessary correction of an agency they say was politicized against the president, while critics view them as retaliation that weakens national security.

stories.headline: School Headscarf Ban Sparks Rare Protests in Azerbaijan and Row With Turkey
stories.summary:
Azerbaijan's education ministry began enforcing new school uniform rules last Monday, turning away girls wearing hijabs and prompting rare protests in Baku and southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad. The rules, approved on September 21, ban clothing that contradicts "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools and do not mention the hijab by name. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on October 6.

The interior ministry said it detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules. A mother protesting in the capital, Shahiza Huseynova, was detained Tuesday, and her husband said she had been told to remove her child's hijab or face prison. Activist Ilkin Huseynov, who launched an online platform offering free lessons to barred pupils, was reportedly taken by unidentified men on Wednesday, and his phone has been off since. Users also report problems reaching Instagram and TikTok without a VPN.

Protests are uncommon in the country of 10.5 million, where President Ilham Aliyev has ruled since 2003 and opposition figures and many independent journalists are jailed. Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and its government strictly enforces that. Most protests have occurred in religiously conservative areas, including districts near the 765km border with Iran.

The dispute has also strained relations with Turkey, Baku's closest ally. Azerbaijan is pulled between Turkey and Iran: over 60% of Azerbaijanis identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni. Authorities have long been wary of religious influence from abroad, and the crackdown suggests they intend to hold firm.

stories.headline: Judge Dismisses Brennan Suit Seeking Records Preservation in 'Grand Conspiracy' Probe
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Washington on Thursday dismissed a lawsuit by former CIA Director John Brennan seeking to compel the Justice Department to take special steps to preserve records in an ongoing criminal investigation. The judge agreed that Brennan did not yet have standing to sue over the probe, which targets him for his role in reviewing the 2016 election.

Brennan filed the suit in July. The investigation has been described as examining what is called a "grand conspiracy" and is viewed by critics as aimed at President Donald Trump's perceived political enemies. Brennan argued that preservation orders were needed to protect evidence in the case.

The ruling does not resolve the underlying investigation. Supporters of the probe say it is a legitimate inquiry into how the 2016 election was reviewed by intelligence officials, while critics call it politically motivated retribution. Because the dismissal rested on standing, Brennan could potentially seek relief again if he faces concrete action such as charges.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Resumes Refinery Strikes as Zelensky Accuses US of Betrayal Over Withdrawn Support
stories.summary:
Ukrainian drones struck a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky declared that a brief pause on strikes against energy sites was over. Zelensky had halted the attacks to comply with a US demand, but said Moscow spurned the truce and continued hitting Ukrainian infrastructure. In an interview with the Financial Times, he angrily accused Washington of a "dangerous" withdrawal of support critical to Ukraine's defense. Russia accused Kyiv of undermining US peace efforts.

The confrontation follows a week of strain over American assistance. Ukrainian officials said Starlink and Starshield satellite services, which underpin battlefield communications and drone operations, were throttled earlier this week. Service was restored to full capacity, a Ukrainian official told Axios, though questions remain about what happened. Elon Musk blamed President Trump for restrictions on the service. Ukrainian officials also told CBS News that American counterparts blamed "bad weather" for a failure of the system used to detect Russian missile launches, an explanation Kyiv did not believe.

The disputes come after a large Russian attack cut power to 600,000 people in Kyiv, despite Trump's announced "energy ceasefire." A Ukrainian drone strike at a Russian refinery also defies Trump's demand that Kyiv stop hitting such facilities. Critics of the administration say Trump has made one-sided concessions to Moscow, including an arrangement to import Russian diesel. Supporters of the president's approach say he is pressing both sides toward negotiations. Separately, the UK is reportedly sending Ukraine more Storm Shadow long-range missiles before winter.

stories.headline: Update: US Producer Prices Jump 1.3% in September, Biggest Monthly Gain Since 2022
stories.summary:
The US producer price index for September rose 1.3% from the previous month, the largest monthly increase since March 2022, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Thursday. Wholesale prices were up 6.3% from a year earlier. Energy prices climbed 10.8% in the month, and the reading came in much hotter than economists expected.

The report follows Wednesday's consumer price data showing inflation at 3.7% over the past year, driven by a gasoline surge tied to conflict in the Middle East and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Wholesale costs often feed through to consumer prices with a lag, raising the prospect of further pressure on households. Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said this week that one more rate hike this year would be appropriate.

The International Energy Agency said Thursday it will complete the release of the remaining 100 million barrels of oil approved in March as part of an effort to curb global fuel prices. Politically, inflation is a central issue before the midterms: a Fox News poll found President Trump's approval on inflation at a new low of 22%. Trump told a Montana rally Wednesday, "We have very little inflation," a claim critics contested while administration allies point to energy shocks from foreign conflicts.

stories.headline: Trump Cancels Hegseth's Plan to Livestream Nidal Hasan Execution
stories.summary:
President Trump announced Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former Army major who killed 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood attack, will not be livestreamed. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote, adding that "many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die." The decision overrules Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who announced earlier this month that the execution would be public.

The plan drew bipartisan criticism. Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin called it "sick," while Republican Sen. John Curtis said it was "not an effective deterrent." Critics also warned the images could be used to fuel radicalization, and faith leaders voiced disgust. Trump said Hasan deserved to be executed but cited the substantial criticism.

Some conservative religious figures supported the idea, including the leader of the CREC church, to which Hegseth belongs, who said he prefers public executions to private ones. The episode has revived debate over capital punishment and the firing squad method, with opponents of the death penalty arguing the case shows the practice's problems and supporters stressing that Hasan's guilt is not in dispute.

stories.headline: Suspicious Letters Sent to Election Offices in Several States Weeks Before Midterms
stories.summary:
Federal authorities are investigating letters containing suspicious substances that were mailed to state election officials and congressional offices across the country. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said Wednesday that US Postal Service investigators blocked delivery of a letter containing a "powdery white substance" to his office. Election officials in three states have reported suspicious packages in the past week.

Several federal agencies, including the FBI and US Capitol Police, are examining "multiple letters containing suspicious substances," according to a notice sent to Senate staff. Recipients have been urged to treat the mailings as potentially hazardous. No injuries or adverse health effects have been reported, and officials said they are working with state and federal law enforcement.

The incidents come only a few weeks before the November midterm elections, when election offices are handling heavy workloads, including mail ballots. Separately, the Justice Department has given California 48 hours to confirm whether noncitizens were mailed ballots, a dispute in which the administration cites election integrity and state officials push back. Authorities have not announced a suspect or motive in the mailings.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says Leak Compromised B-2 Strike on Iran, Declares 'Leakers Should Be Shot'
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said at a rally in Arizona on Wednesday that a leak about the departure and arrival times of U.S. B-2 bombers forced him to call off a planned raid on Iran, and he declared that "leakers should be shot." He said the aircraft flew about 1:00 a.m. and that Iran "was waiting for them." He said the disclosure, which he attributed to reporting by the New York Times and CNN, compromised the mission.

Trump said he spoke with Gen. Dan Caine, who assured him the military could proceed despite the leak. He said he called off the raid, ordered the same timing to be used, and that the strikes took place two days later. "They ought to go to jail," he said of the leaker, adding that the aircraft left Missouri at 12:07.

The remarks come as coverage of the Iran conflict continues across the political spectrum. Right-leaning outlets have emphasized the president's account of operational security failures and his calls for prosecution of leakers. Left-leaning and wire outlets have focused on the violent language and on continuing oil price increases and Saudi-Houthi strikes, amid what is described as a midterm-season pause in the Iran war. Media organizations have generally defended reporting on national security matters as in the public interest, while administration supporters argue such disclosures endanger troops.

The account has not been independently verified, and the Pentagon had not detailed the timeline in the material reviewed. Oil markets and regional strikes between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces remain key developments to watch.

stories.headline: FTC Sends Civil Subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic Over AI Safety Incidents
stories.summary:
The Federal Trade Commission on Wednesday sent civil subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic seeking documents about safety incidents that have escalated into what Axios described as an industry crisis. A person familiar with the matter said the probe focuses on potential consumer protection violations.

The investigation is one of several steps the administration has taken to show a firm hand with AI companies, following multiple incidents involving unreleased models. The demands come amid mounting public concern about the risks posed by frontier AI systems.

The move adds to regulatory pressure on the industry. Eight states recently sued OpenAI alleging it misled users on ChatGPT safety, and Anthropic reported strong financial results this week ahead of a planned listing. Neither company's response to the subpoenas was included in the reporting reviewed.

Civil subpoenas typically require companies to produce internal records, and the inquiry could lead to enforcement action if violations are found. The FTC has not publicly detailed the scope or timeline.

stories.headline: Brazil's Congress Approves Shorter Working Week Ahead of Presidential Runoff
stories.summary:
Brazil's Senate approved a constitutional amendment on Wednesday cutting the standard working week from 44 hours to 40 and guaranteeing two days off weekly without salary cuts. Senators passed it 75 to one, after the Chamber of Deputies approved it in May. It is described as the biggest overhaul of workers' rights since the return to democracy in 1988, and is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers.

The vote came less than two weeks before the 25 October presidential runoff between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro won the first round with 47% to Lula's 45.2%. Polling cited by the BBC shows almost 70% of Brazilians support the change.

Flavio Bolsonaro reversed his earlier opposition and voted yes, saying most workers want an end to the six-day week. Lula called that reversal "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the vote. Critics of the measure warn it will raise production costs and eventually prices, while supporters say more rest will improve productivity.

The change will be phased in, first to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and later to 40, taking more than a year to take full effect.

stories.headline: Two Dead in Istanbul After Heaviest Rainfall in 84 Years
stories.summary:
Two people have died after severe flooding in Istanbul that the governor said was caused by the heaviest rainfall in 84 years. A 14-year-old boy was electrocuted after stepping in a puddle, and a 34-year-old man died after slipping and hitting his head while crossing a road. Authorities are investigating the boy's death.

Deputy Mayor Nuri Aslan said 595 stranded people had been evacuated and more than 8,000 workers were responding. Some areas received rainfall equal to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Cars were submerged, sections of road collapsed, a river burst its banks, and 46 planes were unable to land at Istanbul airports.

Governor Davut Gul told residents to avoid leaving home unless necessary. Schools were ordered closed Thursday and Friday, metro hours were extended to 02:00, and some public employees were granted administrative leave. More than 16 million people live in the metropolitan area, and the interior ministry warned of sudden flooding in several provinces as rain is expected to continue.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Agrees to Hear Trump Administration's Bid to Shield DOGE Records From Disclosure
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court has agreed to take up an appeal from the Trump administration seeking to prevent the disclosure of information about the inner workings of the Department of Government Efficiency, the agency used to downsize the federal government. The case stems from a legal fight with a government watchdog group that sought records about how the agency operated.

The administration argues that the records should be shielded from disclosure, while the watchdog group contends that the public is entitled to information about an entity that made far-reaching changes to the federal workforce and programs. Lower courts had previously sided with the group in ordering some level of disclosure, prompting the administration's appeal to the justices.

The decision to hear the case places a major question about executive branch transparency before the high court. Supporters of the administration say the agency's internal deliberations deserve protection, and critics say the government should not be able to avoid public records obligations for a body that wielded significant authority. The outcome could shape how open-records laws apply to temporary or unconventional White House initiatives.

The court's move comes as the nation heads into the midterm elections, with the administration's use of executive power already a frequent subject of litigation. Arguments are expected to be scheduled in the coming months, with a ruling likely before the end of the court's term.

stories.headline: School Roof Collapse in Pakistan's Peshawar Kills at Least 29, Mostly Children
stories.summary:
The roof of a private school collapsed in Peshawar, in northwestern Pakistan, on Thursday, killing at least 28 children and a female teacher, according to the latest reports. More than 50 other people were injured. Early accounts from an emergency services official had put the toll lower, at 10 children, and the figure rose as rescuers reached more victims.

The building was the Al-Khair Education Centre, a private school in the city. Rescue teams worked through the rubble to search for survivors, and the country's prime minister urged rescuers to speed up their efforts.

The cause of the collapse has not been established. Such incidents in Pakistan have often prompted questions about building safety standards and the oversight of private schools, and officials are expected to open an inquiry. The casualty count may continue to change as the search continues and the injured receive treatment at local hospitals.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV Recovering After Surgery Confirms Lung Cancer Diagnosis
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV is eating and walking as he recovers from surgery that confirmed he has lung cancer, the Vatican said. The 71-year-old American pontiff underwent a 90-minute procedure on Tuesday to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung, and the Vatican described the operation as successful.

There has been no word on whether Leo will be able to keep a planned trip to South America next month. Peru's president said the visit might be in jeopardy as the pope recovers. Catholics across the region responded with prayers and expressions of support, along with concern about whether the first American pope could undertake such a physically demanding journey.

The Vatican has said its bureaucracy is built to function smoothly even when the pope cannot. Further details on his treatment and recovery timeline are expected, along with a decision on his travel plans.

stories.headline: Asian Tech Stocks Plunge as Anthropic Reports Revenue Surge Ahead of Planned Listing
stories.summary:
Technology shares fell sharply across Asia on Thursday amid concerns over AI infrastructure spending and hotter-than-expected US inflation. South Korea's Kospi and Kosdaq were temporarily halted after falling more than 8%, Japan's Nikkei 225 lost close to 5%, Samsung dropped 9.5%, SK Hynix fell 11% and SoftBank slid more than 9%. In the US, chipmakers including AMD, Nvidia and Intel fell sharply on Wednesday.

The selloff followed remarks by Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan, who said many investors have "no clue" and have set extreme expectations, likening it to a casino. Declines deepened after US inflation rose to 3.7% in September, raising fears the Federal Reserve will raise rates further.

Against that backdrop, Anthropic told prospective investors that revenue rose 45% to $16.8 billion in the three months to September, the BBC understands. The company reportedly said it was profitable for a second straight quarter and is laying groundwork for a stock market listing expected before the end of the year. Anthropic declined to comment.

Rival OpenAI has said it will not go public this year. Anthropic's figures offer a gauge of whether the AI industry can finance the infrastructure it requires.
